imp.generic: She was born into difficult circumstances that would shape the rest of her life.
imp.author: They named her after a river nobody could find on any map, and that was the first lie and the kindest one, and she spent the rest of her life being true to water.

imp.generic: The town had a long history of racial violence that everyone tried to forget.
imp.author: The town remembered what it needed to remember and forgot what it could not afford to keep, and the difference between the two was a body, was always a body, cooling in the particular silence that follows a thing done in the open and called nothing.

imp.generic: She grieved deeply for her lost child.
imp.author: She did not cry. Crying was for women who still believed the world owed them an answer. She went instead to the woodpile and split what was already split, and the sound of it was the only word she had left for what had been taken.

imp.generic: He had a complicated relationship with his father, marked by both love and resentment.
imp.author: He loved his father the way you love a scar: with your fingers, in the dark, when nobody is watching, knowing it is yours, knowing it was made.

imp.generic: The old house held many memories for the family.
imp.author: The house knew them. Knew the particular weight of their footsteps on the third stair, knew the smell of their quarrels and their reconciliations, which were nearly the same smell, knew where they hid the things they could not say out loud and kept those things safe in its walls the way a body keeps a bullet: close, and quiet, and not without consequence.

imp.generic: After years of suffering, she finally found a moment of peace.
imp.author: It came to her on a Tuesday, the peace did, small and unannounced as a wren, and she did not reach for it, having learned by then that peace is not caught but only witnessed, only stood beside for the brief time it consents to stay.

imp.generic: The community came together to support one another through hard times.
imp.author: They brought what they had, which was never enough and always enough: a jar of something put up in August, a hand on the shoulder that said I know without saying I know, a body in a chair across the room so the night would not be the only company. This is what they had instead of safety. It was not nothing. Lord, it was not nothing.

imp.generic: She realized that freedom was more complicated than she had imagined.
imp.author: Free. The word sat in her mouth like a stone she did not know how to swallow or spit. Free meant the field was still there. Free meant the road was hers if she could find shoes and if the men on the road decided it was so. Free was a door opened onto another door, and behind that door a woman who looked like her mother was scrubbing a floor that would never be her own. She stood in the word and turned around slowly and could not find the edge of it.

imp.generic: The story of her people was one of endurance and survival.
imp.author: This is what they passed down instead of land: the knowing of how to hold a thing inside the body where no one can legislate it, no one can deed it away. They passed it in the particular way a grandmother braids hair, in the songs that meant one thing to the ones who sang them and another thing entirely to the ones who listened, in the recipe that was never written because writing was a door they had not always been allowed to open. It survived. Not despite them. Inside them. Which is the only place survival ever lives.

imp.generic: In the end, she understood that some wounds never fully heal.
imp.author: She did not heal. Let us not say she healed. Let us say instead that she learned to build her life around the space of it, the way a town builds around a river it cannot bridge and cannot name and cannot stop going down to, in the early morning, before the day requires anything, to stand at the edge of what cannot be crossed and call it, quietly, by its right name.
